Micha Klein, Artificial Beauty “Venus”

A digitally built portrait from Micha Klein’s 1998 series Artificial Beauties: a flawless face in front of floating 3D crystals, lens flares, and electric color.

Context

Kunsthuizen describes an original 1998 photograph from Klein’s series Artificial Beauties, as exhibited at the Groninger Museum: a Cibachrome print on aluminium behind perspex, 75 × 75 cm. Kunsthuizen.

Klein (1964–2026) studied at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie and graduated in 1989 with the first degree there in computer graphics. The Groninger Museum held a ten-year retrospective of his digital work in 1998. Micha Klein: About; Digicult (2006); Metropolis M.

Observed

  • A woman with red hair and bare shoulders faces the viewer; her skin is smooth and even, like a retouched render.
  • Behind her float faceted purple and violet crystals of different sizes, some translucent.
  • The background swirls with electric blue, cyan, magenta, and orange streaks and fractal-like filaments.
  • Small star-shaped lens flares sparkle at the lower left and upper right.

Why it belongs

This is the image side of Y2K: 3D software used for its own sake, with rendered crystals, flares, and a perfected artificial face. The Y2K style record cites Evan Collins, in the Guardian, linking the aesthetic to new CAD tools that allowed layered transparencies and lens flares.

The palette of violet, electric blue, and hot pink matches the style’s accent colors.

Borrow

Use a few floating rendered crystals or gems with sharp facets as background motifs.

Add small four-point sparkle flares at the corners of an image.
